Total net oil-equivalent production, by comparison, was 3.98 million barrels of oil equivalent per day (MMboe/d), down from 4.086 MMboe/d in the year-ago quarter. In the Eastern Mediterranean, Chevron's Tamar optimization project and Leviathan's third gathering line ramped up quickly, supporting record quarterly production in the region. Australia also delivered strong operational reliability. These operational improvements are important because Chevron's gas volumes support its LNG business and provide additional supply to global customers. International upstream gas production was 5.563 Bcf/d, down from 5.674 Bcf/d in the year-ago quarter. Thus, the company-wide production record came alongside mixed regional trends, with stronger U.S. gas volumes and operating gains at key overseas assets. title: Shell Agrees to $1.45 Billion Sale of North West Shelf Stake - The Globe and Mail
content: Shell plcSHEL, through subsidiary Shell Australia Pty Ltd, has agreed to sell its 16.67% non-operated interest in Australia’s North West Shelf (“NWS”) project to subsidiaries of XRG P.J.S.C. The transaction carries a base consideration of $1.45 billion, subject to customary adjustments, along with an additional payment tied to specified milestones. Announced on Nov. 3, 2026, the agreement has an effective date of Jan. 1, 2026, and is expected to close in 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary conditions. The effective date is distinct from the anticipated closing date, which remains dependent on these conditions being met. The divestment is part of Shell’s effort to streamline its portfolio and focus investment on advantaged integrated gas positions. For investors, it shows the company monetizing a mature asset while maintaining its broader commitment to natural gas and liquefied natural gas (“LNG”). Shell’s 16.67% holding is a minority, non-operated interest: it gives the company a share in the project without responsibility for day-to-day operations. The $1.45 billion base consideration will be subject to customary adjustments and could be supplemented by the milestone-linked payment. The buyers will also assume decommissioning obligations and provide security for them. Decommissioning covers the eventual closure or removal of facilities when they are no longer needed. Transferring these responsibilities may reduce Shell’s future exposure to retirement costs, although the benefit depends on the final terms and completion of the deal. The NWS project is an integrated LNG and domestic gas development in Western Australia, involving interconnected joint ventures with Woodside, ChevronCVX, BPBP, Shell, MIMI and CNOOC. Shell’s interest includes upstream assets, pipeline and midstream infrastructure, project companies, offtake arrangements and related petroleum and pipeline interests. Production from NWS’ original gas fields has declined, leaving spare capacity at the Karratha Gas Plant, which processes gas for domestic supply and LNG exports. The project is moving toward a mix of its own resource production and third-party toll processing. Under this model, other producers can pay to use the facility to process their gas, changing the project’s operating and commercial profile. As production from the original fields eases, future plant utilization will increasingly depend on attracting third-party gas volumes and securing toll-processing arrangements. The sale follows Shell’s 2023 divestment from the Browse project, a proposed offshore development intended to send gas to Karratha for processing and export through NWS infrastructure. Together, the transactions indicate a more selective approach to Shell’s Australian gas portfolio, not a complete exit from the country. XRG, an international energy investment company focused on natural gas, chemicals and energy solutions, is adding an established Australian gas position to its broader portfolio through the proposed acquisition. Shell retains a substantial Australian presence through its operated QGC project and Prelude floating LNG facility, the Crux development, and joint venture interests in Arrow Energy and Gorgon. These positions preserve its exposure to Australian gas production, LNG supply and infrastructure after the NWS sale. Globally, Shell expects to grow LNG sales by 4-5% annually through 2030. The NWS divestment is therefore a portfolio reallocation: Shell is reducing its stake in one mature project while continuing to invest in other gas and LNG assets. The company has not indicated a change to its long-term LNG growth target. The milestone-linked payment could add to the base consideration, but it is contingent and should not be treated as guaranteed. The expected 2027 closing remains subject to regulatory approvals and other conditions, so investors should monitor progress and any changes to the timetable. Investors should watch how Shell deploys the proceeds and whether its remaining Australian projects support the group’s LNG plans. The sale also involves a trade-off: after completion, Shell will no longer participate in NWS production or any upside from higher third-party processing volumes. The final financial contribution will depend on completion, customary adjustments and any contingent payment. The transfer of decommissioning responsibilities also changes Shell’s future obligations tied to the asset. Overall, the North West Shelf sale demonstrates Shell’s focus on portfolio quality and disciplined capital allocation. The deal provides a $1.45 billion base value and reduces the company’s exposure to a mature, non-operated project, while Shell retains several important Australian gas and LNG assets. The recommendations of Wall Street analysts are often relied on by investors when deciding whether to buy, sell, or hold a stock. Media reports about these brokerage-firm-employed (or sell-side) analysts changing their ratings often affect a stock's price. Do they really matter, though? Before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage, let's see what these Wall Street heavyweights think about Chevron (CVX). Chevron currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.59, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 29 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.59 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy. Of the 29 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 20 are Strong Buy and three are Buy. Check price target & stock forecast for Chevron here>>> The ABR suggests buying Chevron, but making an investment decision solely on the basis of this information might not be a good idea. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation. Do you wonder why? As a result of the vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover, their analysts tend to rate it with a strong positive bias. According to our research, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations for every "Strong Sell" recommendation. In other words, their interests aren't always aligned with retail investors, rarely indicating where the price of a stock could actually be heading. Therefore, the best use of this information could be validating your own research or an indicator that has proven to be highly successful in predicting a stock's price movement. Zacks Rank, our proprietary stock rating tool with an impressive externally audited track record, categorizes stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), and is an effective indicator of a stock's price performance in the near future. Therefore, using the ABR to validate the Zacks Rank could be an efficient way of making a profitable investment decision. In spite of the fact that Zacks Rank and ABR both appear on a scale from 1 to 5, they are two completely different measures. The ABR is calculated solely based on brokerage recommendations and is typically displayed with decimals (example: 1.28). In contrast, the Zacks Rank is a quantitative model allowing investors to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5. It has been and continues to be the case that analysts employed by brokerage firms are overly optimistic with their recommendations. Because of their employers' vested interests, these analysts issue more favorable ratings than their research would support, misguiding investors far more often than helping them. On the other hand, earnings estimate revisions are at the core of the Zacks Rank. And empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements. In addition, the different Zacks Rank grades are applied proportionately to all stocks for which brokerage analysts provide current-year earnings estimates. In other words, this tool always maintains a balance among its five ranks. Another key difference between the ABR and Zacks Rank is freshness. The ABR is not necessarily up-to-date when you look at it. But, since brokerage analysts keep revising their earnings estimates to account for a company's changing business trends, and their actions get reflected in the Zacks Rank quickly enough, it is always timely in indicating future price movements. title: Chevron Advances Iraq Oilfield Deal, Expands Growth Prospects - TradingView
content: Chevron Corporation CVX is moving closer to expanding its footprint in Iraq, potentially strengthening its international production opportunities and long-term growth prospects. Iraq's Ministry of Oil announced that it had reached an agreement with Chevron on key provisions of the development contract for the West Qurna 2 oil field. The progress sets the stage for a formal agreement by the end of 2026, according to Iraqi News, The development represents an important step in Chevron's efforts to establish a stronger presence in Iraq's oil industry. Alongside West Qurna 2, the company is exploring opportunities involving the Nasiriyah oil field and four additional exploration blocks, potentially creating a broader platform for future investment. The latest progress followed a meeting between Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair and Chevron's vice president of business development, Joe Cook, on Nov. 3. Discussions focused on the West Qurna 2 oil field and opportunities to deepen cooperation between the two parties. Although significant portions of the development contract have been agreed upon, the final agreement remains pending. Both sides are targeting completion and formal signing by the end of 2026, providing a potential timeline for Chevron's expanded involvement in the project. West Qurna 2 represents a strategically important opportunity for Chevron, given Iraq's substantial hydrocarbon resources and the potential to expand international production. Greater involvement in the country's oilfields could strengthen the company's upstream portfolio and provide additional opportunities to deploy its technical capabilities. However, the project's contribution to Chevron's production and earnings will depend on the final contractual terms, investment requirements, development schedule and operational execution. Additional Opportunities Could Expand Chevron's Iraq Presence Chevron's discussions with Iraq extend beyond West Qurna 2. The two sides have agreed to continue negotiations regarding the Nasiriyah oil field and four additional exploration blocks. These potential agreements could broaden Chevron's exposure to Iraq's upstream sector, creating opportunities to participate in multiple development and exploration projects. A larger portfolio in the country could also provide greater flexibility in allocating capital across assets with different development timelines. For Chevron, international projects remain an important component of its long-term growth strategy. The company can potentially leverage its experience in complex oilfield development, reservoir management and production technology to support operations in Iraq. Nevertheless, exploration opportunities typically involve geological uncertainty, substantial upfront investment and longer development periods. Their financial benefits may not materialize immediately, making the eventual project terms and investment commitments important considerations for investors. Iraq's renewed engagement with Chevron comes as the government attempts to attract additional foreign investment and strengthen its energy infrastructure. Over the past six months, the country has increased cooperation with U.S. and other international energy companies to improve production capabilities, modernize facilities and address operational challenges. The Iraqi government has also expressed willingness to support Chevron and other American energy companies by reducing investment obstacles and facilitating greater participation in the oil and gas sector. Khudair highlighted the importance of American expertise in oilfield development, technology transfer and workforce training. These priorities could give Chevron opportunities to contribute beyond production growth, particularly through operational improvements and developing local technical capabilities. For Iraq, stronger partnerships with international operators could help improve the efficiency of its oil industry and support its efforts to overcome infrastructure and export-related constraints. Iraq's efforts to attract international energy investment are taking place amid significant challenges in oil transportation. Interruptions to shipments associated with the Strait of Hormuz blockade have increased pressure on the country's energy sector, highlighting the importance of maintaining reliable export channels and strengthening production infrastructure. title: Chevron Earnings Call Highlights Cash, Growth and Resilience - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron ((CVX)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call. Chevron’s Earnings Call Signals Strong Momentum Despite Market Risks Chevron’s earnings call carried a strongly positive tone, led by robust cash generation, a stronger balance sheet, steady production and record refining and natural gas output. Management also highlighted AI gains and broad growth opportunities, although lower sequential earnings, volatile commodity prices, permitting issues and a future non-cash accounting loss remain notable risks. Chevron reported third-quarter earnings of $9.9 billion, or $5.06 per share, while adjusted earnings reached $10.4 billion, or $5.28 per share. Cash flow from operations excluding working capital was $16.6 billion, and adjusted free cash flow totaled $14.2 billion. Chevron reduced debt by more than $3 billion and increased cash by more than $4 billion during the quarter. Net debt to cash flow from operations improved to 0.4 times, giving the company greater financial flexibility. Third-quarter production was nearly 4 million barrels of oil equivalent per day despite entitlement impacts and planned maintenance turnarounds. U.S. upstream output stayed above 2 million barrels per day for the fifth consecutive quarter. Chevron posted record quarterly natural gas production of more than 9 billion cubic feet per day, led by Australia and the Eastern Mediterranean. Its U.S. Gulf of America operations also set a new quarterly deepwater production record. Permian production remained above 1 million barrels per day for a sixth straight quarter. Capital spending per barrel improved by more than 25%, while drilling and completion spending fell 40% and facility spending declined 50%. Chevron expanded its acreage and secured new fiscal terms in Venezuela, making the business more competitive and immediately accretive to free cash flow. The company plans to double production from its three joint ventures to about 600,000 barrels per day by 2031, with total costs below $20 per barrel. Chevron is on track to reach roughly 300,000 barrels per day of gross Venezuelan production by year-end, up 20% in 12 months. It markets all crude from the three ventures, with most volumes shipped to U.S. refineries. A planned 50% reduction in Bakken midstream tariffs should improve returns, expand economic inventory and increase operating flexibility. Chevron plans to reduce its rig count from three to two while sustaining about 180,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. The Hess Midstream restructuring is expected to increase corporate return on capital employed by 0.5% and deconsolidate $3.7 billion of debt. Chevron also expects recurring earnings and an immediate improvement in Bakken upstream earnings and cash flow after the transaction. Chevron achieved record crude throughput across its refining system and record quarterly U.S. crude throughput. More than 80% of U.S. refinery turnarounds over the past two years were completed with first-quartile duration, supporting reliability. A proprietary catalyst at Chevron’s largest U.S. refineries lifted distillate production by 10% after changes to cut points. Third-quarter distillate yield at those refineries reached 46%, while Pascagoula recorded its strongest diesel production in at least three or four years. Chevron accelerated debottlenecking at Pasadena, adding about 15% of refinery capacity at nominal cost. The company also plans to increase Pascagoula capacity by another 7% by 2030. Upstream debottlenecking projects added more than 85,000 barrels per day of capacity. TCO’s third-generation plant gained 20% of capacity, Ballymore rose 7%, and Anchor increased capacity by 33%, or 25,000 barrels per day. Chevron added 22 million acres over the past two years, doubling its exploration footprint across 12 new basins. In the latest quarter, it added six Gulf of America blocks as well as acreage in Angola, Nigeria, Guinea-Bissau and Egypt. The company made 15 infrastructure-led discoveries over two years with a 40% success rate, above the industry average. AI pattern recognition found more than 150 leads in the Gulf of America, with 16 prospects advancing to evaluation and 30 net new prospects identified. Chevron said AI generated more than $100 million of value capture year to date in 2026. In the DJ Basin, the technology cut loss-production events by 50%, while AI-enabled production optimization is now deployed in the Permian, Bakken and PZ assets. Chevron’s ApEx system uses four petabytes of data and a century of company knowledge to assemble basin information in hours rather than months. ScoutAI can build basin assessments in hours instead of weeks and is now deployed in 10 new basins. Advanced Chemicals increased cumulative oil-equivalent production in the Permian by as much as 23% during the first 12 months. Chevron is also testing next-generation chemistry through field pilots to improve recovery further. Predictive maintenance, centralized data and AI-supported decisions helped keep Australian LNG reliability strong. Gorgon and Wheatstone operated above nameplate capacity, and the combined assets delivered record third-quarter production. Chevron reaffirmed its framework of consistent dividend growth, efficient investment, a strong balance sheet and share repurchases through the cycle. The company has raised its dividend for 39 consecutive years and plans to keep annual buybacks in the $2.5 billion-to-$3 billion range. Organic capital expenditures totaled $3.9 billion in the quarter. Fourth-quarter spending is expected to rise in line with seasonal trends, but full-year capital expenditures are still expected to finish at the low end of annual guidance. Project Kilby is a 2.67-gigawatt, behind-the-meter power project in West Texas backed by a 20-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft. Chevron is targeting a final investment decision, first power in 2028 and full energization in 2031, with potential expansion to combined-cycle power. Chevron said terms in Iraq currently appear more attractive than they have historically and that it is working with the ministry on a development plan. The company is also discussing similar opportunities with several Middle Eastern governments, building a pipeline of growth options beyond 2030. A significant share of Chevron’s fleet is owned or covered by long-term charters agreed before the conflict, at pre-conflict rates. Controlled transportation and greater use of equity crude, which has reached about 50% at times at certain refineries, are supporting current results. Adjusted third-quarter earnings were $1.6 billion below the prior quarter. The decline shows that strong operating performance did not fully offset a less favorable pricing and timing environment. Adjusted upstream earnings fell because of lower realizations, reduced liftings and unfavorable timing effects. Lower depreciation, depletion and amortization expenses and tax benefits partly offset those pressures. Working capital was negatively affected by sharp commodity price increases late in the quarter. Management said rising prices can create additional timing effects, while those impacts generally unwind when prices fall. When the Hess Midstream transaction closes, Chevron expects a one-time non-cash after-tax loss of $3 billion to $4 billion. Management emphasized that the charge reflects deconsolidation accounting rather than the underlying economics of the deal. Management cited a $64 intra-quarter price spread, with crude prices ranging from $68 to $132 per barrel during the quarter. Chevron said the volatility has not changed its short-term capital allocation approach. Chevron expects refining margins to eventually moderate as refinery runs recover and exports increase. Petrochemical markets could also return to oversupply as trade flows normalize, although margins may remain somewhat elevated through year-end and possibly into next year. Project Kilby requires additional permits beyond those already being pursued. Chevron must also secure financing and finalize its engineering, procurement and construction contract before reaching a final investment decision. Discussions over extending the TCO concession have continued for more than a year across technical, commercial and legal matters. The remaining issues have narrowed to fundamental points, and Chevron said further updates will follow after significant milestones. Chevron expects fourth-quarter capital spending to increase while finishing the year at the low end of its annual range, and it plans to maintain $2.5 billion to $3 billion in buybacks. Venezuela production is targeted at about 600,000 barrels per day by 2031, while Bakken activity will shift to two rigs and long-lateral drilling is expected to exceed 85% in 2027. The Hess Midstream transaction is expected to close at the end of the fourth quarter and carry a $3 billion-to-$4 billion non-cash loss. Chevron also plans to raise exploration spending by 50% from last year’s baseline, potentially drill about 20 wells annually, expand Pascagoula by 7% by 2030, and bring Kilby to first power in 2028, subject to permits and financing. Chevron’s call presented a company generating substantial cash while improving its balance sheet and expanding production, refining and exploration opportunities.
